summary:
Costa Rica decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1971 and, in 2020, became the first Central American country to adopt marriage equality. For a trans visitor this is the region's most permissive legal setting, backed by institutions that operate rather than merely exist.

Legal gender recognition is administrative. Executive Decree 41173-MP, in force since 2018, allows a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. The state health system funds gender-affirming care.

The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised near-universal health coverage and specific protective legislation while recording her concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups. She recommended intersectional data collection as a basis for addressing it.

Policy headwinds are real. A conversion-therapy prohibition bill has been stalled in committee since its 2019 report. In 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education programme and the 2022 anti-LGBT bullying protocol, withdrawing two of the main preventive frameworks in schools.

Detention is the clearest gap between policy and practice. In June 2017 the Justice Ministry, then under Vice-Minister Marco Feoli, announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual could choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility, with relocation decided case-by-case alongside prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners and an exclusive module was under consideration, with Spain's model cited. Reporting in June 2019 found a trans woman, Stephanie, held at CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility where staff said only men are held, and she described identity-targeted abuse including a rape with a broomstick-handle at La Reforma in Alajuela witnessed by a custodian. The Justice Ministry told the outlet there were 23 transgender people in the national prison system at the time.

Official posture has generally been supportive and has drawn organised opposition. The government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia in 2008, when President Óscar Arias and Health Minister María Luisa Avila directed public institutions to facilitate and support activities directed at the eradication of homophobia. In May 2014 President Luis Guillermo Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial on equal mast with the national flag for 17 May, prompting lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and other conservative parties to call it a provocation while a same-sex civil union bill was pending.

Partner protections extend into social security: survivor's pensions were extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans (Ministry of Labor announcement of 25 June 2016, first individual survivor benefit approved 29 June 2018), with the teachers' separate budget excluded.
tangentialFactors:
Opposition to LGBT equality is organised and parliamentary rather than street-level. Conservative lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and allied parties attacked the presidential rainbow flag in 2014 as a provocation, and the conversion-therapy bill has been held in committee since 2019 — a legislature that contains a durable blocking bloc even where the executive and courts move ahead.

The 2025 repeal of the comprehensive sex-education programme and of the 2022 anti-LGBT bullying protocol sits alongside the stalled conversion-therapy bill as the main indicators of rollback pressure. These affect school environments rather than visitors directly, but they signal the direction of domestic policy debate.

The UN Special Rapporteur's 2023 country visit placed Costa Rica among states praised for near-universal coverage, and her concern about discrimination was framed for marginalised groups generally rather than as a finding specific to trans people.

A 2000 Supreme Court ruling held IVF unconstitutional; GayLawNet records it in the context of partnership benefits rather than as a trans-specific rule.

The survivor's-pension extension for same-sex partners, announced in 2016 and applied from 2018, shows benefits machinery reaching same-sex couples, but the teachers' pension budget was excluded, so coverage is not uniform across public schemes.
localsOnly:
Residents can obtain a legal gender marker change on identity documents administratively under Executive Decree 41173-MP (2018), with no surgery and no court order required.

The state health system funds gender-affirming care for residents. The UN Special Rapporteur recommended that the authorities collect intersectional data to measure and address discrimination against LGBT and gender-diverse people in access to services.

The Justice Ministry's 2017 circular allows trans prisoners to request placement in a facility matching their gender identity, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists, and ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners; an exclusive trans module was under consideration, modelled on Spain's protocols for vulnerable prison populations developed with CEJIL since 2016.

Residents with same-sex partners are entitled to survivor's pensions under all national-budget pension plans, following the Ministry of Labor announcement of 25 June 2016 and approval of the first individual survivor benefit on 29 June 2018; the teachers' separate budget remains outside the scheme.

Since 2008 the state has officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia, with directions to public institutions to support activities directed at the eradication of homophobia. The comprehensive sex-education programme and the 2022 anti-LGBT bullying protocol were scrapped by authorities in 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the post-2018 document process also alters the sex marker on all identity documents, or only the name and photograph, is not resolved by the sources held here; Outright International states only that gender change on documents is possible without surgery or court order.

The practical implementation of the 2017 prison placement policy after 2019 is not sourced beyond the CRHoy reporting of that year, which documented a trans woman held in a men's facility. The 23 transgender prisoners cited by the Justice Ministry is a June 2019 figure and has not been refreshed.

The ILGA World Database entry for Costa Rica is held as a reference link but its individual indicators are not itemised in the inventory, so no claim here rests on it.

Enforcement of anti-discrimination law against trans people, and any screening of gender markers at ports of entry, are not documented in the sources supplied; the UN Special Rapporteur's discrimination findings are stated at the level of marginalised groups generally.

The current status of the stalled conversion-therapy bill beyond its 2019 committee report, and the legal instrument used to scrap the 2025 sex-education programme and anti-bullying protocol, remain unresolved.
